sweep_summary: All seven title-hit items in this search of works with stress in the title target are spurious Glottolog attachments to wari1268 — none concerns Wari'. Pamies Bertrán 1997 (already in our per-language bibliography) was checked via its Dialnet abstract: an acoustic study of stress in seven European languages; the other six (Gouskova & Roon on Russian, Speyer on English, Bao on Singapore English, three duplicate records of Mazzola's Romance chapter) name their language in title or venue and were not downloaded. The wari1268 Glottolog list carries the compilation of unrelated 'clash' titles (also Givón 1970, Hopper 1997, Garmendia 2014) that our bibliography inherited and should drop. The catalog's classification (fixed-strict, word-final, domain word) is confirmed by three primary sources now all with a : Everett & Kern 1997 full text (3.3.2.4 'Stress falls on the last syllable of the word..', p. 406 = print 417; 3.3.2.1 sentence-level hierarchy with primary stress on the verb's final syllable), MacEachern, Kern & Ladefoged 1997 (STRESS, p. 25: phrase main stress on the last syllable of the verb or verbal compound; explains Gordon's '(of phrase)' row), and Apontes 2015 (2.6 'Acento', p. 39: 'padrão acentual fixo.. sempre no final da palavra', heavy final syllable required, for the northern Oro Waram dialect). No new source supersedes Everett & Kern; this search of works with stress in the title adds no new statement beyond a fuller locator. Not obtained: Angenot-de-Lima & Angenot 2000 'Sistema prosódico Panchapakura de demarcação lexical' (ILLA 1, CNWS Leiden; the source Apontes cites for detail — medium priority, would refine at family level) and Maeda 2000 Oro Eo MA thesis (low).

new_statements.quote: Stress falls on the last syllable of the word, except when that syllable is a stress-avoiding member of a verbal compound, in which case stress will go on the syllable to its immediate left. [3.3.2.1:] Within the sentence, the final syllables of major lexical categories are stressed. Primary stress in the sentence normally falls on the final syllable of the verb, with final-syllable stress on other lexical categories interpreted as secondary stress. Other morphemes, e.g. verbal inflectional clitics and inflected forms of the preposition, carry tertiary (or even quartiary) stress
new_statements.citation: Everett, Daniel L. & Barbara Kern (1997). Wari': The Pacaas Novos Language of Western Brazil. London: Routledge (Descriptive Grammars); author-posted full text, LingBuzz 001707.
new_statements.locator: Section 3.3.2.4 'Position of stress', p. 406 of the e-book pagination (running header 'Wari' 406', PDF page 419 of the LingBuzz scan; StressTyp2 cites print p. 417), the text; and 3.3.2.1 'Role of stress in the language', p. 404, the text
new_statements.reading: Fixed word-final stress on every lexical word, no lexical contrast, no tone (3.3.3 'There is no distinctive use of pitch'); cues are loudness and raised pitch (3.3.2.2). Above the word there is a sentence-level hierarchy in which the verb's (or verb compound's) final syllable carries primary stress and other words' final stresses are secondary; emphasis can move primary stress to another constituent. The 'stress-avoiding member of a verbal compound' exception (examples 815a-e, e.g. pin 'completely') governs which member of a verb compound carries the primary stress, not the position of stress inside a word. This confirms the catalog's fixed-strict final coding with domain word, and it explains the StressTyp2 (word) / Gordon '(of phrase)' split: MacEachern, Kern & Ladefoged 1997 (p. 25) instrumentally describe only the phrasal main-stress layer, and Apontes 2015 (p. 39) independently reports fixed final stress for the northern Oro Waram dialect.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: Coding fixed-strict final (final stress, domain word) rests on Everett & Kern 1997 section 3.3.2.4, verified verbatim in the full text we hold ( l.16744; p.419 = e-pagination 406 = print p.417). The one stated exception (stress-avoiding members of verbal compounds, e.g. pin 'completely', written as separate words in E&K's examples 815a-e) concerns which element of a verb compound carries primary phrasal stress, not the position of stress within a word, so word-final coding stands. MacEachern, Kern & Ladefoged 1997 (instrumental, held) and Apontes 2015 (downloaded now, northern dialect: 'padrão acentual fixo.. sempre no final da palavra', p.39) independently confirm. Only housekeeping remains: the record's quote/cite/loc/grade fields are empty although the verified primary quotation sits in sources/the domain quotation; promote it and set a primary-verified grade. no reclassification.

sources.quote: 'As palavras em Oro Waram têm padrão acentual fixo, pois o acento se situa sempre no final da palavra. Portanto, não há distinção fonológica com base no acento. Este é previsível no fim da palavra e requer que a sílaba final da palavra seja pesada.' (p. 39); 'a acentuação ocorre sempre na última sílaba da palavra, o acento também não é distintivo' (p. 15); compounds: 'Nas palavras compostas, a proeminência acentual também será realizada no fim da construção' (p. 39); a light final syllable is lengthened under stress (p. 40, 56).

sources.citation: MacEachern, Margaret R., Barbara Kern & Peter Ladefoged (1997). Wari' phonetic structures. Journal of Amazonian Languages 1(1): 3-28.
sources.quote: The major stress in a Wari' phrase is on the last syllable of the verb or verbal compound; secondary stresses appear on other syllables. The following examples show the location of main stress, indicated by underlining, moving steadily away from the beginning of the sentence as the verbal compound is lengthened in various constructions. In the final example, kep kep ?araJirapa? is an embedded sentence; na 'consent' is the verb, so it is na that bears main stress.
sources.locator: section STRESS, p. 25 (scan page numbers, the text); the text
sources.note: Section STRESS (p. 25): main stress in the phrase sits on the last syllable of the verb or verbal compound, with secondary stresses on other syllables; examples show main stress migrating rightward as the verbal compound is lengthened; in an embedded-sentence example the matrix verb na 'consent' bears main stress. Instrumental confirmation of the phrasal layer described in E&K 3.3.2.1; does not contradict word-final stress (it only locates the phrase's main stress). Refines: the 'final' is the verb's final syllable at phrase level, word-final elsewhere.

sources.citation: Ladefoged, Peter and Everett, Daniel L. (1996). The status of phonetic rarities. Language 72. pp. 794-800.
sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.note: The work is entirely about the voiceless apico-dental plosive + voiceless bilabial trill [tB] of Wari' and Oro Win: its lexical frequency (about two dozen Wari' words from Kern's unpublished dictionary), articulation, acoustics, and feature status. The words 'stress', 'accent' and 'tone' do not occur in the paper (WPP pp. 8-12). It therefore says nothing usable about the catalog entry (fixed final stress; secondary only in compounds/reduplications/phrases; no tone) and cannot confirm or contradict it.
